title: The man who lived in the present

lines.text: For 55 years, one man lived almost entirely in the present moment. He could not form new memories.
His name was Henry Molaison. Scientists knew him only as H.M.
In 1953, a surgeon removed parts of both sides of his brain to stop his severe epilepsy.
Including most of a structure called the hippocampus.
The seizures improved. But his memory span shrank to about 30 seconds.
He could meet a researcher, and minutes later greet her as a stranger.
Yet he got better at a tricky drawing task with practice, without remembering ever doing it.
That proved there's more than one kind of memory in the brain.
After he died in 2008, his brain was cut into 2,401 slices, so science could keep learning from him.

sources.claim: Henry Molaison (H.M.): 1953 bilateral medial temporal lobectomy for epilepsy, removing much of both hippocampi; severe anterograde amnesia with ~30 s memory span; improved at mirror drawing (Brenda Milner); died 2008 aged 82; brain cut into 2,401 slices in 2009

publish.title: The Man Who Couldn't Make New Memories 🧠
publish.description: After surgery in 1953, Henry Molaison lived with a 30-second memory for 55 years. He changed what we know about the brain.
publish.pinned_comment: Could you live with a 30-second memory? 👇
